title: The Weather of the coast road
premise: Lior Lockridge returns to the fog-bound coastal town of Vessing for their mother's funeral, where a stranger named Ada Kell greets the family by their old, erased name — Lockridge being a name bought decades ago to buy belonging. As Lior translates the mother's final letters from a dying dialect, they uncover how their father traded language, land, and loyalty for a seat at the town's table, and how Ada's family paid the price. When the council votes to reroute the last bus that still reaches the old neighborhood, Lior must choose between the polished smile that ends conversations and a public reckoning. The novel ends with Lior reading the letters aloud in the original tongue at the final bus stop, saying goodbye properly — and walking home along the coast road as one of them again.
about_author: Mara Eriksen grew up between two fishing towns whose names changed on every new map, and worked for years as an interpreter before turning to fiction. She writes about borders that live inside families rather than on maps.

chapters.title: The Smile That Ends Conversations
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. Returning to Vessing for the funeral, Lior deploys the practiced smile through condolences while feeling the town's dialect slip further out of reach with each borrowed word. At the graveside, grief is performance. Emotional beat: numb displacement, the ache of being fluent in everything except home.

chapters.title: A Name Nobody Uses
chapters.summary: Ada Kell's POV. At the wake, Ada addresses the family by their original name — Vessel — and watches the room go cold. She has waited thirty years to say it aloud. Lior follows her out into the rain, hungry and afraid. Emotional beat: a crack in the coffin-lid of family myth.

chapters.title: Letters in a Dying Tongue
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. Sorting the mother's effects, Lior finds letters written in the old dialect, half-legible even to them. Translating slowly, they learn the mother kept records: dates, sums, names. Emotional beat: intimacy with the dead through language, and the first suspicion that the family's respectability was purchased.

chapters.title: The Table at the Harbor Hotel
chapters.summary: Uncle Bram's POV. Bram, keeper of the family's standing, recalls how Lior's father bought the Lockridge name and a seat among the harbor magnates — and what the Kells lost when the seawall contract went elsewhere. He warns Lior away from Ada. Emotional beat: complicity dressed as protection.

chapters.title: What the Seawall Took
chapters.summary: Ada's POV. Ada shows Lior the drowned fields behind the new seawall, her family's land, and gives them her half of the correspondence — the father's replies to her grandmother, polite, evasive, damning. Emotional beat: shared inheritance of a wound; reluctant alliance.

chapters.title: Borrowed Words
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. A council notice announces the bus route to the old neighborhood will be rerouted after the equinox. Lior, translating the mother's last letter, finds she knew everything and stayed silent to keep her children safe. Lior's smile begins to fail in public. Emotional beat: anger curdling into purpose.

chapters.title: The Vote
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs interwoven. At the council meeting, Bram defends the reroute as progress; Ada speaks the Vessel name into the record and is shouted down. Lior stands but cannot yet speak, and hates themselves for it. Emotional beat: rising tension, the cost of hesitation made public.

chapters.title: Equinox Eve
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. On the last night before the vote is finalized, Lior finishes translating the mother's final letter — an apology addressed not to the Kells but to Lior, asking them to say what she could not. Bram offers Lior his seat at the table if they let it go. Emotional beat: temptation at its most seductive; identity at the crossroads.

chapters.title: The Last Bus
chapters.summary: Climax. Lior's POV. At the final stop on the doomed route, before councilors and neighbors, Lior reads the letters aloud in the old tongue — stumbling, then steady — naming the father's bargain and the mother's silence, and greeting Ada by name. Bram walks out; others stay. Emotional beat: catharsis; the smile finally abandoned for a real voice.

chapters.title: Weather of the Coast Road
chapters.summary: Resolution. Ada's POV. Weeks later, the route survives on appeal, and the town must learn to say two names for one family. Lior stays through winter, teaching the dialect to anyone who comes. Walking the coast road together through changing weather, they belong nowhere perfectly and here completely. Emotional beat: quiet, earned peace.
